# SK2121 — The `as` operator tests a conversion that always succeeds

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The operand already converts to the tested type implicitly, so `as` can only return the operand and the `null` it appears to guard against is the operand’s own `null`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `TryCastAlwaysSucceeds` (`resharper_try_cast_always_succeeds_highlighting`) |

## Why

`d as Base` where `d` is a `Derived` yields `d`, always. The operator reads as a question — *is this a `Base`?* — and there is no question: the widening is the same one an assignment would perform. What it costs is the null check that usually follows, which the next reader takes for a type guard and which is really a null guard on a value the code may already have proved non-null. ⚠ **This is the half of issue #1 the compiler does not already own, and it is the only half.** The always-*false* cases are compiler diagnostics: `s is int` and `d is Unrelated` are `CS0184`, `d as Unrelated` is `CS0039`, and an unreachable type pattern in a `switch` is `CS8121` — the last two are errors, not warnings. `v is int` on an `int` is `CS0183`. What is left over is this operator, which the compiler permits in silence because it is well defined.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
void M(Derived d) {
    var b = d as Base;
    if (b is null) { return; }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
void M(Derived d) {
    var b = (Base)d;
}
```

## When it does not fire

The conversion must be an identity, an implicit reference or a boxing conversion as `ClassifyConversion` reports it; anything else — an explicit conversion, a user-defined one, an unboxing — is a conversion that can genuinely fail and is not reported. ⚠ **Type parameters are excluded outright.** `t as Base` inside a generic method is classified against the constraint set and not against the type the method is instantiated with, so a conversion that looks certain there is not certain at run time. `dynamic` operands, error types and an operand with no type at all are declined for the same reason. The fix keeps the expression’s static type rather than removing the operator: a widening becomes the matching cast, `(Base)d`, so a surrounding `var` still declares a `Base`, and only an identity conversion — where the operand already has the tested type — is replaced by the operand itself. `fixIsSafe` is `true` because both edits are the conversion the operator was already performing.
